YELLOW-DOG CONTRACT PROHIBITION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes a specific, narrow rule of California law: the prohibition on requiring, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, a promise about whether Jane Doe will or will not join or remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization. This rule is codified at California Labor Code §§ 920-923, sometimes referred to by the older term "yellow-dog contract" prohibition. It states facts about what that statute declares void, what conduct it makes a misdemeanor, and how a related federal statute treats the same subject. It is not itself a labor organization membership agreement, a union authorization card, a collective bargaining agreement, or a determination that any particular promise, policy, or practice at Acme Inc. does or does not violate this law. It does not tell Jane Doe or Acme Inc. what to do about any particular hiring decision, employment application, or workplace dispute. It is also distinct from this project's Restriction on Requiring Arbitration as a Condition of Employment information sheet, which describes a different California statute (Labor Code § 432.6) addressing a different condition an employer might try to impose at hiring — arbitration agreements, not labor organization membership.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "PROMISE"
The chapter containing this prohibition opens with a definitions section. It gives the word "promise," as used throughout the chapter, a deliberately broad meaning: the term covers not only a formal promise but also an undertaking, contract, or agreement, and it applies regardless of whether that promise, undertaking, contract, or agreement was written or oral, or express or implied. This means the prohibition described in the following clauses is not limited to a signed document — an oral or implied understanding between an employer and an employee or applicant can fall within the same statutory definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "includes promise, undertaking, contract, or agreement, whether written or oral, express or implied."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 920 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, chapter definition of "promise" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=920.)
  Known gap: This section defines "promise" but does not define "labor organization" or "employer organization" anywhere in this chapter of the Labor Code — those terms are used throughout §§ 921-923 without a chapter-specific statutory definition, so their scope (for example, whether a given professional association or works council would qualify) is not resolved by this chapter's text alone. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

CORE PROHIBITION ON UNION-MEMBERSHIP PROMISES
California law declares that a promise made after August 21, 1933, between an employee or prospective employee and an employer, prospective employer, or any other person, is contrary to public policy if either party promises any of three things: (a) to join or remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization; (b) not to join or not to remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization; or (c) to withdraw from an employment relation if the person joins or remains a member of a labor organization or an employer organization. The statute's own text covers both directions — a promise to join a labor organization and a promise not to join one are both listed as contrary to public policy — and it applies at the hiring stage ("prospective employee," "prospective employer") as well as during an existing employment relationship.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every promise made after August 21, 1933, between any employee or prospective employee and his employer, prospective employer or any other person is contrary to public policy if either party thereto promises any of the following:(a) To join or to remain a member of a labor organization or to join or remain a member of an employer organization,(b) Not to join or not to remain a member of a labor organization or of an employer organization,(c) To withdraw from an employment relation in the event that he joins or remains a member of a labor organization or of an employer organization."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 921 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, promises against public policy regarding labor organization membership (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=921.)
  Known gap: The statute declares such a promise "contrary to public policy"; it does not, in this section's own text, create a private civil cause of action for damages against an employer who extracts such a promise — the consequence the statute's own text spells out is addressed in the next clause. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing Labor Code §§ 921-923 was attempted for this document and returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law confirming or narrowing this reading of the statute's plain text has been checked here.

THE PROMISE PROVIDES NO BASIS FOR COURT RELIEF
The same statutory section that lists the three prohibited promises also states the specific legal consequence for them: such a promise does not afford any basis for a court to grant legal or equitable relief against a person who made it, and it likewise does not afford a basis for relief against any other person who advises, urges, or induces either party to disregard the promise — so long as that advice, urging, or inducement is given without fraud or violence or a threat of fraud or violence. In effect, the statute makes the promise itself legally inert: an employer cannot go to court to enforce it, and a person who counsels an employee to break such a promise is protected from suit over that advice under the same statutory sentence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Such promise shall not afford any basis for the granting of legal or equitable relief by any court against a party to such promise, or against any other persons who advise, urge, or induce, without fraud or violence or threat thereof, either party thereto to act in disregard of such promise."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 921 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, unenforceability of a prohibited labor-organization-membership promise (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=921.)
  Known gap: The statute's carve-out withdrawing this protection when a person's advice, urging, or inducement involves "fraud or violence or threat thereof" is not itself defined further in this chapter's text — where the line falls between protected advice and disqualifying conduct is not answered by the statute's own words. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular advice given to any particular reader falls on one side of that line or the other.

COERCION AS A CONDITION OF EMPLOYMENT IS A MISDEMEANOR
A separate section of the same chapter addresses active coercion rather than a mere promise: it makes it a crime for any person, agent, or officer to coerce or compel another person to enter into a written or verbal agreement not to join or become a member of any labor organization, when that coercion is used as a condition of securing employment or of continuing in employment. The statute's own text classifies this conduct as a misdemeanor. Unlike the preceding section, which addresses the promise itself and its unenforceability in court, this section addresses the act of coercing or compelling someone to make such a promise, and attaches criminal liability to that act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any person or agent or officer thereof who coerces or compels any person to enter into an agreement, written or verbal, not to join or become a member of any labor organization, as a condition of securing employment or continuing in the employment of any such person is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 922 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, misdemeanor for coercing a promise not to join a labor organization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=922.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text names the conduct a misdemeanor but does not, in this section, specify a fine amount, a jail-term range, or which government office is responsible for charging it — those particulars, if any apply specifically to this section, are not stated in the text of Labor Code § 922 itself and were not independently researched for this document. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular person's conduct meets or fails to meet this section's definition of coercion or compulsion.

THE STATUTE'S OWN DECLARATION OF PUBLIC POLICY
The same chapter closes its core prohibition with the Legislature's own explanation of the policy behind it. The statute's text states that negotiation of terms and conditions of labor should result from voluntary agreement between employer and employees, and — after describing employers' ability to organize into corporate and other forms of capital control, and the individual unorganized worker's resulting difficulty in exercising real liberty of contract — declares that it is necessary for an individual worker to have full freedom of association, self-organization, and choice of representatives to negotiate the terms and conditions of employment, free from an employer's interference, restraint, or coercion in that self-organization or in other concerted activities for collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "it is necessary that the individual workman have full freedom of association, self-organization, and designation of representatives of his own choosing, to negotiate the terms and conditions of his employment, and that he shall be free from the interference, restraint, or coercion of employers of labor, or their agents, in the designation of such representatives or in self-organization or in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 923 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, declared public policy favoring freedom of association and self-organization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=923.)
  Known gap: This section is framed by its own text as an interpretive aid — "in the interpretation and application of this chapter, the public policy of this State is declared as follows" — rather than as a standalone operative rule with its own separate remedy; how much independent legal weight this declaration carries beyond interpreting §§ 921 and 922 is a question this document does not resolve, and a CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this section returned a rate-limit error (quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law on that question was checked here. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

COMPARISON TO THE FEDERAL NATIONAL LABOR RELATIONS ACT
Separately from this California statute, a federal law — the National Labor Relations Act — also addresses discrimination tied to union membership in hiring and employment. It makes it an unfair labor practice for a covered employer, by discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment, to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization. Unlike the California statute described in the preceding clauses, which voids the prohibited promise and criminalizes coercion to obtain it, the federal statute is enforced through a different mechanism entirely: an unfair-labor-practice charge processed by the National Labor Relations Board, not a state civil-void doctrine or a state misdemeanor prosecution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "by discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(3) (National Labor Relations Act) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(3), unfair labor practice to discriminate regarding hire to encourage or discourage union membership (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/158)
  Known gap: The National Labor Relations Act's coverage has statutory exclusions — for example, for agricultural laborers, domestic-service workers, and independent contractors, defined in a different section of the same federal title (29 U.S.C. § 152) — that were not independently fetched or verified for this document, so this clause does not state whether any particular reader's work relationship falls inside or outside federal NLRA coverage. This document also does not attempt to resolve any question of whether or how federal law might preempt or coexist with the California statute described elsewhere in this document for a particular employer; a CourtListener search for judicial decisions on that preemption question returned a rate-limit error (quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law on it was checked here. This is a federal statute, described here only as a separately confirmed comparison point — not a claim about which law, state or federal, governs any particular reader's situation.
